analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the ban in March 2013 and put it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it; a companion amendment failed 40 to 60 in April.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess many semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns defined by their features or model names, along with ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Weapons lawfully owned before enactment would be grandfathered, and private transfers of those weapons would have to go through a licensed dealer for a background check. It would also fund voluntary buy-back programs and require a federal study of mass shootings.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the people it aimed to protect were those exposed to mass shootings, which the bill's backers said were increasingly carried out with the semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines it banned. It also would have given police the same access to these weapons as before while closing the civilian market for new ones.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons defined by feature lists or named models, including AR-15 and AK-type rifles.
Bans the manufacture and sale of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices that accept more than 10 rounds, and requires serial numbers and manufacture dates on covered weapons and devices.
Grandfathers weapons lawfully owned before enactment, so current owners would not have had to surrender them, and funds buy-backs through existing justice grants.

Requires private transfers of grandfathered weapons to go through a licensed dealer running a background check, and directs the Justice Department to study the causes of mass shootings and report to Congress.
Requires the Attorney General to keep a public record of the make and model of any banned weapon used in a crime.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers would lose the civilian market for the banned rifles, pistols, shotguns, and magazines, which include some of the most popular and profitable models sold. Some lawful gun owners would face new restrictions: they could no longer buy the banned weapons or large magazines, and selling or giving a grandfathered weapon would require a dealer-run background check.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, sellers, and some owners

drawbacks.text: Because the bill grandfathered every weapon lawfully owned at enactment, the millions of banned rifles and high-capacity magazines already in circulation would have remained legal, limiting how much the ban could do on its own.

The ban is defined largely by features such as pistol grips, folding stocks, and barrel shrouds rather than by how a weapon fires, a design critics said targets cosmetics and was easy for manufacturers to design around.

Studies of the earlier 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban generally found its effect on overall gun crime was modest, an honest cost an supporter would weigh against the hope of reducing mass-shooting casualties (general knowledge).
The transfer rule would have required even a gift of a grandfathered weapon between two lawful, unlicensed owners to run through a licensed dealer, adding cost and paperwork to legal transactions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case was preventive: it could not remove weapons already owned, so its value depended on shrinking the future supply of the rifles and large magazines used in recent mass shootings, at a real cost to an industry and to buyers of those guns. Its weaknesses were that grandfathering left the existing stock untouched and that feature-based definitions invite workarounds, so its practical effect would likely have been gradual rather than immediate.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Judiciary Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar in March 2013, but Majority Leader Harry Reid never brought it up for a vote because it clearly lacked the 60 votes needed to cut off debate; when a companion assault-weapons amendment reached the floor on a separate bill that April, it failed 40 to 60.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Feinstein on January 24, 2013, weeks after the Sandy Hook shooting, with 24 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.
The Judiciary Committee held three sets of hearings in January and February 2013, then on March 14, 2013 ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
It never received a floor vote; the chamber's leader declined to schedule it because supporters could not muster the 60 votes needed to end debate.
When a similar assault-weapons amendment was offered on the floor in April 2013 on a separate gun bill, it failed 40 to 60, with all Republicans and more than a dozen Democrats voting no.
The bill sat on the calendar until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers kept the semiautomatic rifle and high-capacity magazine market fully open; the debate itself coincided with a widely reported surge in sales of the very rifles the bill targeted. Opponents of new federal restrictions also gained, having stopped the ban without any senator having to cast a recorded vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers; ban opponents

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican sponsored the bill; the committee reported it on party lines, and on the floor in April 2013 the companion amendment drew 40 yes votes from Democrats and 60 no votes from all Republicans plus over a dozen Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would criminalize manufacturing the named AR-15 and AK-type rifles, many pistols and shotguns, and all large-capacity magazines, cutting off the industry's fastest-growing civilian product lines. Its defeat preserved that market, and the 2013 debate itself drove a widely reported buying surge.

Dealers would have lost sales of banned weapons and magazines, but the bill would have routed every private transfer of a grandfathered weapon through a licensed dealer running a background check, sending them fee-generating transaction volume.
The bill bans import, sale, and manufacture of magazines holding more than 10 rounds and requires marking and forfeiture provisions for them, eliminating that product line in the civilian market.
